clue.text: Egghead's IQ absent crossing local hilltop

indicators.note: the hilltop word lies across the other pieces, holding them in its middle

parts.note: a knoll is a small hill or mound in the neighbourhood
IQ measures intelligence, and wit is a word for intelligence
A is the standard abbreviation for absent, as in a register

explanation.surface: A clever person, absent-minded, wanders across a nearby hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' means the hill word straddles the others, so they sit in its middle; 'absent' gives A by the register convention.
explanation.definitionFit: An egghead is an intellectual, and a know-it-all is someone who presents themselves as knowing everything.

clue.text: For 5/7 of 21, The Mystic Author's written up melody

indicators.note: in a down clue, written upwards means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: a pen is a writer or author, especially in journalism
a melody is a tune

explanation.surface: A mysterious author's tune has been put on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is HOLSTER; five of its seven letters give HOLST, the composer of The Planets, whose movement 'Neptune' is subtitled 'The Mystic'. 'written up' turns PEN into NEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Holst's suite The Planets has a movement named after the eighth planet, carrying the subtitle The Mystic.

clue.text: Hypocrite's holiday schedule arranged with dodgy rep

parts.note: Whit, short for Whitsun, is a Christian holiday in Britain

indicators.note: the schedule letters are put in a new order along with the others

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so these letters are jumbled too

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A two-faced holiday plan is drawn up together with a shady sales representative.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'arranged' and 'dodgy' signal jumbling. The phrase comes from Matthew 23, where Jesus likens hypocrites to whitewashed tombs.
explanation.definitionFit: A whited sepulchre is a biblical image for a person who looks virtuous outside but is corrupt within, a pretender to goodness.

clue.text: One building puzzle for Noah? Either of two puzzles

definitions.text: One building puzzle for Noah? Either of two puzzles

parts.words: One building puzzle for Noah? Either of two puzzles
parts.note: the phrase names a famous disc-stacking puzzle, and read another way is a building whose city name is a word puzzle (an anagram) made from Noah and One

explanation.surface: A riddle about a structure for Noah that could be one of two brainteasers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tower of Hanoi is a puzzle of moving discs between pegs; separately, HANOI is NOAH plus I (one) rearranged, so the 'tower' is a building whose name is a puzzle for Noah.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase denotes a classic mathematical game of moving rings between three pegs, and also, punningly, a tower in a city whose name scrambles a patriarch's name.

clue.text: Indicators from new motorist engaged in crazy spell on circuit

indicators.note: going round in a circuit means the jumbled letters run around the short piece
crazy means wild or deranged, signalling that the letters of spell are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
to be at something is to be engaged in it, as in being at work

explanation.surface: A learner driver loses the plot and goes wild during laps of a racetrack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' scrambles the five letters to LPLES, which 'on circuit' runs round the pair. In Britain learner drivers must show red L on white plates front and back.
explanation.definitionFit: Learner drivers in the UK display signs bearing a red letter L to warn others of their inexperience.

clue.text: Our urge is to reform, putting squeeze on power

definitions.text: Our urge is to reform, putting squeeze on power

parts.note: to press is to squeeze

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the letters of our urge are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: A campaigning body says its aim is change, achieved by leaning on those in authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reform' scrambles the first two words to UREGROU. The whole clue also describes what such a lobby group does.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobby or campaign organisation seeks to change policy by applying influence to people in government.

clue.text: Understand instructions to Vincenzo Peruggia?

explanation.surface: Telling an art thief what to do.
explanation.walkthrough: Vincenzo Peruggia stole the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in 1911, so 'grab the painting' is what he would be told.
explanation.definitionFit: To grasp a situation is an idiom for comprehending it; read literally, the words tell someone to fetch a painting, as the Louvre thief did.

clue.text: Fall out on a large scale, as tears zip!

definitions.text: Fall out on a large scale

explanation.surface: Weeping as if your trousers were being done up.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, tears are drops and zips are flies, so the phrase can mean 'drops, like flies' — tears behaving as zips do.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to die or collapse in great numbers; punningly, tear-drops behave like the fly of a pair of trousers.

clue.text: What you have to do to get this pop music mag

definitions.text: What you have to do to get this pop music mag

parts.words: What you have to do to get this pop music mag
parts.note: read as an instruction, the magazine's title tells you to strike blows hard, and doing so would give the title

explanation.surface: Asking how to obtain a particular music magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Smash Hits was a British pop magazine (1978-2006); its name, read as a verb phrase, says to deliver smashing blows.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of a popular British music magazine doubles as an instruction to strike forcefully.

clue.text: Sports coach relocated in Preston

indicators.note: relocated means moved to a new place, so these letters are put in new positions

explanation.surface: A trainer has moved to the Lancashire town of Preston.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relocated' rearranges IN PRESTON. Preston is a city in Lancashire, northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A professional player who teaches racket sport at a club is a kind of sports coach.

clue.text: Is king cross about his failing?

indicators.note: about means around, so the hybrid animal goes round the other pieces

parts.note: a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Asking whether a monarch is angry about his own shortcomings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like an adjective meaning angry; it is the noun for a hybrid, MULE, which goes 'about' IS and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad government is the typical failing of a monarch, so poor rule is a king's failing.

clue.text: Group of pop acts better, in essence

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so each word gives its letters without the first and last

explanation.surface: A band's performances are better at heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The cores of POP, ACTS and BETTER are O, CT and ETTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of eight performers or musicians is a group, especially in chamber music.

clue.text: Cargo of rum "acquired" by ship's master, brought to book

indicators.note: the strange word is taken on board inside the ship abbreviation, like cargo

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
rum is an old-fashioned British word for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A ship's captain is said to have obtained a load of rum, and is held to account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rum' looks like the drink but means strange; it is the 'cargo' the steamship takes on. Wackford Squeers is the cruel schoolmaster in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's tyrannical headmaster of Dotheboys Hall is a schoolmaster who exists in a novel.

clue.text: Second of revellers heading back towards the Rising Sun

indicators.note: the second letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: astern means going backwards, towards the rear of a ship

explanation.surface: A party-goer heads back home toward Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: The second letter of 'revellers' is E. 'The Rising Sun' looks like Japan, but here it is simply the direction of sunrise.
explanation.definitionFit: The sun rises in the east, so going towards it is heading in that direction.

clue.text: Organ partly responsible for debilitative arthritis

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, a run across the two words

explanation.surface: A body part is to blame for crippling joint disease.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of 'debilitative' into the start of 'arthritis'.
explanation.definitionFit: The hearing apparatus is a sense organ of the body.

clue.text: With the ale drunk, soft drink remains in the glass

indicators.note: drunk suggests something jumbled and unsteady, so the letters of the ale are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
p is piano, the musical direction for soft

explanation.surface: Once the beer is finished, only a little soft drink is left in the glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges THE ALE into HEELTA, then P. 'soft drink' looks like one phrase, but 'soft' is P and 'drink' starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The dregs or last drops of liquor left at the bottom of a glass are called by this old word.

clue.text: Jack and John turned up in Turkey wanting list of functions

indicators.note: the reversed sailor and lavatory go inside the country abbreviation

parts.note: TR is the international vehicle registration code for Turkey

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the pair is written bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, and AB (able seaman) is one
john is slang for a toilet, as is loo

explanation.surface: Two men named Jack and John arrived in Turkey lacking a schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' gives OOLBA. 'Jack' and 'John' look like men's names but are a sailor and a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: In software, a strip of icons gives access to a program's commands.

clue.text: Source of Vanilla Ice's initial chords? Wrong

indicators.note: wrong suggests the letters are out of order and need fixing
the first letter of the rapper's name is taken

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rapper's opening chords sound off-key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vanilla Ice' looks like the rapper's name, but Vanilla is the spice. 'initial' takes I from Ice's, and 'Wrong' rearranges I + CHORDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanilla flavouring comes from the pods of a climbing tropical plant of this flower family.

clue.text: Nurse restrains party bore

indicators.note: to restrain is to hold in, so the word for nurse holds the party

parts.note: to nurse is to care for
Lib is short for the Liberal party

explanation.surface: A nurse holds back a tedious party guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' looks like a tedious person; it means the inner diameter of a gun barrel.
explanation.definitionFit: The inside diameter of a gun barrel is its gauge, measured as this.

clue.text: Resistance involved in Corporation smear, causing commotion

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped up within, so R goes inside the belly word

parts.note: corporation is a humorous old word for a pot belly, a tum
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
to oil something is to smear it with grease

explanation.surface: Opposition in a council over a smear campaign causes uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a council or company; it is a jocular word for a paunch, TUM.
explanation.definitionFit: Turmoil is a state of great disturbance or confusion, a synonym for uproar.

clue.text: Gaining little land for oneself, break gunman's cover

indicators.note: the break word gains another piece added at its end

parts.note: hols, short for holidays, is a British word for a break
Ter. is an abbreviation for territory, a piece of land

explanation.surface: A man grabs some land for himself and then breaks a gunman's cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Hols is British informal for holidays.
explanation.definitionFit: A leather case worn on the hip to carry a pistol protects or covers the weapon.

clue.text: Appointed to work in pub or jail

explanation.surface: Taken on as bar staff, or sent to prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Bar staff work behind the bar, so being placed there is literally being put behind bars.
explanation.definitionFit: To imprison someone is to lock them up; literally, a person placed to serve drinks stands at the back of the bar counter.

clue.text: Indulgent type, note, taking in a dance

indicators.note: taking in means containing, so the banknote holds the dance

parts.note: a fiver is a five-pound note
a reel is a lively Scottish dance

explanation.surface: A pleasure-seeker pays a banknote to get into a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: A fiver is British slang for a five-pound note; REEL goes inside it after F.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lives without restraint, enjoying food and drink, is a self-indulgent sort.
